cultures.summary: Before the adoption of Hellenistic Greek astronomy, Arabian astronomers mapped the equatorial night sky through the figure of Al-Jawza' ('The Central One'), a crowned queen adorned with a belt of pearls.
cultures.historicalContext: In pre-Islamic Arabian and early Bedouin tradition documented by Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi (903–986 CE) in his Book of Fixed Stars (Kitāb Ṣuwar al-Kawākib), the stars around the celestial equator formed Al-Jawza'. Unlike the Hellenistic Greek hunter Orion, Al-Jawza' was an ancient feminine celestial figure. Her three belt stars were Nizam al-Jawza' ('The String of Pearls'), her feet were Rigel and Saiph, and her right hand was Betelgeuse (Ibt al-Jawza', which later entered European astronomical nomenclature via medieval translation errors as Betelgeuse). The rising and setting of these stars governed the anwa' seasonal calendar and desert night navigation.
cultures.contrastWithIAU: Al-Jawza' is strictly NOT an Arabic translation of the Greek Orion. While European astronomers later conflated Orion with Al-Jawza', indigenous Arabic tradition conceptualized an entirely separate female monarch figure, with distinct mythical associations and desert navigational markers.

cultures.summary: In classical Chinese astronomy, the equatorial stars form Mansion Shen (参宿, 'Three Stars'), the 21st lunar lodge and supreme military commander of the Western White Tiger.
cultures.historicalContext: As the central constellation of the Western White Tiger (西方白虎) recorded in the Han dynasty Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian by Sima Qian) and the Song dynasty star charts, Shen (参) originally signified the three brilliant belt stars (Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka) before expanding to encompass the surrounding quadrilateral. In Chinese imperial astrology, Shen represents the Great General or Commander-in-Chief of the empire's armed forces, with the outer stars representing his vanguard, flank officers, and military banners. Shen is famously paired in Chinese literature with the Mansion of the Heart (Xin, 宿心, centered on Antares in Scorpius): because Shen and Xin lie on opposite sides of the celestial sphere, they never appear in the night sky simultaneously, inspiring Du Fu's classic poem on long-separated friends: 'Like Shen and Shang in the evening sky, we move through life without ever meeting.'
cultures.contrastWithIAU: Shen is completely distinct from the Western hunter Orion. It functions as a lunar lodge (xiù, 宿) along the celestial equator and an imperial military tribunal rather than a heroic mythological figure. Furthermore, its astronomical orientation is aligned with Chinese equatorial coordinates (polar distance and right ascension hours) rather than Hellenistic ecliptic coordinates.
